# Solution

**Answer: Yes.** The Laurent series of $f$ has no negative coefficients.

## Proof

Let $A = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : r < |z| < R\}$ (with $0 \le r < R \le \infty$; the general case reduces to this by translation). Since $f$ is holomorphic on $A$, it admits a unique Laurent expansion convergent on $A$:

$$f(z) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k\, z^k.$$

Likewise, each $F_n$ holomorphic on $A$ has a unique Laurent expansion

$$F_n(z) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k^{(n)}\, z^k,$$

convergent on $A$. Termwise differentiation of a Laurent series is valid on its annulus of convergence and yields another convergent Laurent series on the same annulus. Differentiating $n$ times:

$$F_n^{(n)}(z) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k^{(n)}\,(k)_n\, z^{k-n}, \qquad (k)_n := k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1).$$

Reindexing with $j = k - n$ (so $k = j+n$):

$$F_n^{(n)}(z) = \sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty} c_{j+n}^{(n)}\,(j+n)_n\, z^{j}.$$

The hypothesis $F_n^{(n)} = f$ and uniqueness of the Laurent expansion give, for every $j \in \mathbb{Z}$,

$$a_j = c_{j+n}^{(n)}\,(j+n)_n. \tag{$\ast$}$$

**Key observation.** The falling factorial $(j+n)_n = (j+n)(j+n-1)\cdots(j+1)$ vanishes precisely when one of the factors $j+1, j+2, \dots, j+n$ equals $0$, i.e., precisely when

$$j \in \{-1, -2, \dots, -n\}.$$

For each such $j$, equation $(\ast)$ forces

$$a_j = c_{j+n}^{(n)} \cdot 0 = 0.$$

Hence, for every positive integer $n$,

$$a_{-1} = a_{-2} = \cdots = a_{-n} = 0. \tag{$\ast\ast$}$$

Now let $m < 0$ be any negative integer. Taking $n = -m$ (a positive integer) in $(\ast\ast)$, we obtain $a_m = 0$. Since $m < 0$ was arbitrary,

$$a_k = 0 \quad \text{for all } k < 0.$$

Therefore the Laurent series of $f$ contains only non-negative powers of $z$; it has no negative coefficients. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
